concepts.title: Axial tilt and sunlight angle
concepts.summary: Earth's tilted axis, not its distance from the Sun, causes the seasons by changing the angle of sunlight; the noon Sun altitude rule quantifies it.

keyPoints.statement: Earth's axis is tilted 23.5 degrees from the perpendicular to its orbital plane.

evidence.quote: Earth's axis is tilted 23.5 degrees from the perpendicular to its orbital plane.

keyPoints.statement: The axis keeps pointing in the same direction in space all year, toward Polaris.

evidence.quote: The axis keeps pointing in the same direction in space all year, toward the star Polaris.

keyPoints.statement: Seasons are caused by the tilt of the axis, not by Earth's distance from the Sun.

evidence.quote: Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, not by Earth's distance from the Sun.

keyPoints.statement: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January and farthest in early July.

evidence.quote: In fact, Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, at about 147.1 million km, and farthest in early July, at about 152.1 million km.

keyPoints.statement: A high Sun concentrates energy on a small area; a low Sun spreads the same beam over a larger area.

evidence.quote: When the Sun is high in the sky, sunlight hits the ground steeply and its energy is concentrated on a small area.

keyPoints.statement: Noon altitude = 90 - |latitude - declination|, with declination +23.5, 0 and -23.5 on the June solstice, equinoxes and December solstice.

evidence.quote: noon altitude = 90 - |latitude - declination|

keyPoints.statement: Sunlight intensity on flat ground is the full beam intensity times the sine of the Sun's altitude.

evidence.quote: The intensity of sunlight on flat ground equals the full beam intensity multiplied by the sine of the Sun's altitude.

misconceptions.description: Thinks the seasons happen because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer and farther in winter.
misconceptions.beliefStatement: It is summer when Earth is closer to the Sun, and winter when it is farther away.
misconceptions.correction: The tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of Northern Hemisphere winter.

evidence.quote: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during Northern Hemisphere winter.

misconceptions.description: Thinks Earth's axis tips back and forth during the year.
misconceptions.beliefStatement: Earth's axis tips toward the Sun in summer and tips away in winter.
misconceptions.correction: The axis keeps pointing in the same direction in space all year; only Earth's position in its orbit changes.

evidence.quote: Only Earth's position in its orbit changes.

misconceptions.description: Thinks sunlight intensity is proportional to the Sun's altitude angle, so a 30 degree Sun gives a third of the full beam.
misconceptions.beliefStatement: A Sun at 30 degrees gives a third of the full sunlight, because 30 is a third of 90.
misconceptions.correction: Intensity follows the sine of the altitude, so a 30 degree Sun gives half of the full beam.

evidence.quote: At an altitude of 30 degrees the ground receives half of the full beam intensity, because sin 30 = 0.5.

misconceptions.description: Drops the minus sign of southern latitudes when using the noon altitude rule.
misconceptions.beliefStatement: For a southern city I can use its latitude as a positive number in the noon altitude rule.
misconceptions.correction: Southern latitudes are negative, and the sign matters when you subtract the declination.

evidence.quote: Northern latitudes are positive and southern latitudes are negative.

concepts.title: Day length
concepts.summary: Day length changes with latitude and season because of the tilt, not because Earth's spin changes; the hottest weather lags the longest day.

keyPoints.statement: On the equinoxes, day and night are each about 12 hours long everywhere on Earth.

evidence.quote: On the equinoxes, day and night are each about 12 hours long everywhere on Earth.

keyPoints.statement: At the equator, day length stays close to 12 hours all year.

evidence.quote: At the equator, day length stays close to 12 hours all year.

keyPoints.statement: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has days longer than 12 hours; the hemisphere tilted away has shorter days.

evidence.quote: Away from the equator, the hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has days longer than 12 hours and the hemisphere tilted away has days shorter than 12 hours.

keyPoints.statement: The difference from 12 hours grows with latitude.

evidence.quote: The difference grows with latitude.

keyPoints.statement: North of the Arctic Circle the Sun does not set on the June solstice (24 hours of daylight).

evidence.quote: North of the Arctic Circle, at latitude 66.5, the Sun does not set at all on the June solstice, giving 24 hours of daylight.

keyPoints.statement: Earth's spin rate does not change with the seasons.

evidence.quote: Earth takes about 24 hours to spin once, and this spin rate does not change with the seasons.

keyPoints.statement: The longest day is not the hottest day: seasonal lag delays the heat by several weeks.

evidence.quote: The longest day of the year is not the hottest day.

misconceptions.description: Thinks days are longer in summer because Earth spins more slowly.
misconceptions.beliefStatement: Days are longer in summer because Earth spins more slowly then.
misconceptions.correction: Earth's spin rate does not change with the seasons; the tilt changes how much of each latitude circle is in sunlight.

evidence.quote: Earth's spin rate does not change with the seasons.

misconceptions.description: Thinks the longest day of the year is also the hottest.
misconceptions.beliefStatement: The longest day of the year is the hottest day.
misconceptions.correction: The hottest weather comes several weeks after the solstice because of seasonal lag.

evidence.quote: The hottest weather comes several weeks later because of seasonal lag.

concepts.title: Opposite hemispheres
concepts.summary: The hemispheres have opposite seasons, split by the equator and not by east or west.

keyPoints.statement: The two hemispheres always have opposite seasons.

evidence.quote: The two hemispheres always have opposite seasons.

keyPoints.statement: The June solstice starts summer in the Northern Hemisphere and winter in the Southern Hemisphere.

evidence.quote: The June solstice is the start of summer in the Northern Hemisphere and the start of winter in the Southern Hemisphere.

keyPoints.statement: On the December solstice the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn and the Southern Hemisphere has its longest days.

evidence.quote: The Sun is directly overhead at latitude -23.5, the Tropic of Capricorn, and the Southern Hemisphere has its longest days.

keyPoints.statement: The dividing line is the equator, not a line between east and west.

evidence.quote: The dividing line is the equator, not a line between east and west.

keyPoints.statement: Two cities at the same latitude have the same season, wherever they are in longitude.

evidence.quote: Two cities at the same latitude have the same season even if they are on opposite sides of the world.

keyPoints.statement: On the equinoxes neither hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun.

evidence.quote: On the equinoxes neither hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun.

misconceptions.description: Thinks it is summer everywhere on Earth at the same time.
misconceptions.beliefStatement: When it is summer, it is summer everywhere on Earth at the same time.
misconceptions.correction: The two hemispheres always have opposite seasons.

evidence.quote: The two hemispheres always have opposite seasons.

misconceptions.description: Thinks the seasons are opposite between the eastern and western halves of the world.
misconceptions.beliefStatement: Seasons are opposite in the eastern and western halves of the world.
misconceptions.correction: The dividing line is the equator, not a line between east and west.

evidence.quote: The dividing line is the equator, not a line between east and west.

materialItems.text: Find the noon Sun altitude in Boston (latitude 42) on the June solstice.
materialItems.solution: The declination is +23.5. The difference between latitude and declination is 42 - 23.5 = 18.5. The noon altitude is 90 - 18.5 = 71.5 degrees.

evidence.quote: Find the noon Sun altitude in Boston (latitude 42) on the June solstice.

materialItems.text: Find the noon Sun altitude in Boston (latitude 42) on the December solstice.
materialItems.solution: The declination is -23.5. The difference is 42 - (-23.5) = 65.5. The noon altitude is 90 - 65.5 = 24.5 degrees. The Sun is much lower in December, so sunlight is spread out and weaker.

evidence.quote: Find the noon Sun altitude in Boston (latitude 42) on the December solstice.

chunks.text:
# Why Earth Has Seasons

Earth Science 101, Unit 4 handout. Read the three sections in order, then try the practice problems. Angles are in degrees and distances are in millions of kilometers (million km).

## 1. Axial tilt and sunlight angle

Earth's axis is tilted 23.5 degrees from the perpendicular to its orbital plane. The axis keeps pointing in the same direction in space all year, toward the star Polaris. Because the direction of the tilt stays fixed while Earth orbits, each hemisphere leans toward the Sun for part of the year and away from it for the rest.

Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, not by Earth's distance from the Sun. In fact, Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, at about 147.1 million km, and farthest in early July, at about 152.1 million km. The Northern Hemisphere has winter when Earth is closest to the Sun.

The tilt matters because it changes the angle of sunlight. When the Sun is high in the sky, sunlight hits the ground steeply and its energy is concentrated on a small area. When the Sun is low in the sky, the same beam of sunlight is spread over a larger area, so each square meter receives less energy.

The noon Sun altitude is the angle of the Sun above the horizon at local noon. To find it, use this rule:

noon altitude = 90 - |latitude - declination|

The declination is the latitude where the Sun is directly overhead at noon. The declination is +23.5 on the June solstice, 0 on the equinoxes, and -23.5 on the December solstice. Northern latitudes are positive and southern latitudes are negative.

The intensity of sunlight on flat ground equals the full beam intensity multiplied by the sine of the Sun's altitude. At an altitude of 30 degrees the ground receives half of the full beam intensity, because sin 30 = 0.5.

### Worked example 1.1

Find the noon Sun altitude in Boston (latitude 42) on the June solstice.

Solution: The declination is +23.5. The difference between latitude and declination is 42 - 23.5 = 18.5. The noon altitude is 90 - 18.5 = 71.5 degrees.

### Worked example 1.2

Find the noon Sun altitude in Boston (latitude 42) on the December solstice.

Solution: The declination is -23.5. The difference is 42 - (-23.5) = 65.5. The noon altitude is 90 - 65.5 = 24.5 degrees. The Sun is much lower in December, so sunlight is spread out and weaker.

### Practice problems 1

1. What is the tilt of Earth's axis, in degrees? Answer: 23.5

2. What is the main cause of Earth's seasons?
   - A. Earth's distance from the Sun changes during the year
   - B. The tilt of Earth's axis
   - C. The Sun gives off more energy in summer
   - D. Earth spins faster in summer

   Answer: B

3. True or false: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. Answer: True

4. Find the noon Sun altitude at latitude 30 on the June solstice, in degrees. Answer: 83.5

5. Find the noon Sun altitude at latitude 50 on an equinox, in degrees. Answer: 40

6. The Sun is at an altitude of 30 degrees. What fraction of the full beam intensity reaches flat ground? Answer: 0.5

7. How much farther from the Sun is Earth in early July than in early January, in million km? Answer: 5

## 2. Day length

Day length is the number of hours between sunrise and sunset. Earth takes about 24 hours to spin once, and this spin rate does not change with the seasons. What changes is how much of each latitude circle is in sunlight.

On the equinoxes, day and night are each about 12 hours long everywhere on Earth. At the equator, day length stays close to 12 hours all year. Away from the equator, the hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has days longer than 12 hours and the hemisphere tilted away has days shorter than 12 hours.

The difference grows with latitude. On the June solstice, a city at latitude 40 gets about 15 hours of daylight, while a city at latitude 60 gets about 18.5 hours. North of the Arctic Circle, at latitude 66.5, the Sun does not set at all on the June solstice, giving 24 hours of daylight.

Long days add to the heating effect of steep sunlight. In summer a location gets more intense sunlight and gets it for more hours, so summer is warmer for two reasons.

The longest day of the year is not the hottest day. The ground and oceans keep warming for several weeks after the June solstice, so the hottest weather in the Northern Hemisphere usually comes in July or August. This delay is called seasonal lag.

### Worked example 2.1

A city at latitude 40 has 15 hours of daylight on the June solstice. How many hours of night does it have on that date, and how much longer is the day than the night?

Solution: A full day is 24 hours, so the night is 24 - 15 = 9 hours long. The day is 15 - 9 = 6 hours longer than the night.

### Practice problems 2

1. How many hours of daylight does the equator get on the December solstice? Answer: 12

2. True or false: On an equinox, a city at latitude 60 and a city at latitude 20 have about the same day length. Answer: True

3. Why are days longer in summer?
   - A. Earth spins more slowly in summer
   - B. The Sun moves more slowly across the sky in summer
   - C. More of your latitude circle is in sunlight when your hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun
   - D. Earth is closer to the Sun in summer

   Answer: C

4. A city has 9 hours of daylight on the December solstice. How many hours of night does it have? Answer: 15

5. Put these places in order from shortest to longest day on the June solstice: latitude 60, the equator, latitude 40, latitude 70. Answer: the equator, latitude 40, latitude 60, latitude 70

6. In which month is the Northern Hemisphere's hottest weather most likely: June, July, or December? Answer: July

## 3. Opposite hemispheres

The two hemispheres always have opposite seasons. When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted away from it. The June solstice is the start of summer in the Northern Hemisphere and the start of winter in the Southern Hemisphere.

On the December solstice the situation is reversed. The Sun is directly overhead at latitude -23.5, the Tropic of Capricorn, and the Southern Hemisphere has its longest days. That is why December is a summer month in Australia, Argentina, and South Africa.

The dividing line is the equator, not a line between east and west. Two cities at the same latitude have the same season even if they are on opposite sides of the world. Tokyo and San Francisco are both in the Northern Hemisphere, so they have summer at the same time.

On the equinoxes neither hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun. The Sun is directly overhead at the equator, and both hemispheres receive the same amount of sunlight.

### Worked example 3.1

Find the noon Sun altitude in Sydney (latitude -34) on the December solstice.

Solution: The declination is -23.5. The difference is -34 - (-23.5) = -10.5, and its absolute value is 10.5. The noon altitude is 90 - 10.5 = 79.5 degrees. The Sun is high in the sky, so December is summer in Sydney.

### Practice problems 3

1. It is the June solstice. What season is starting in Argentina? Answer: winter

2. True or false: When it is summer in Canada, it is also summer in Australia. Answer: False

3. On which date is the Sun directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn?
   - A. The June solstice
   - B. The March equinox
   - C. The December solstice
   - D. The September equinox

   Answer: C

4. Find the noon Sun altitude at latitude -34 on the June solstice, in degrees. Answer: 32.5

5. Tokyo (latitude 36) and San Francisco (latitude 38) are on opposite sides of the Pacific Ocean. True or false: they have summer at the same time. Answer: True

6. Which two things are true on the December solstice? Select all that apply.
   - A. The Southern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun
   - B. The Northern Hemisphere has its longest day
   - C. The Sun is directly overhead at latitude -23.5
   - D. Earth is at its farthest point from the Sun

   Answer: A and C

## Common mistakes

> **Common mistake:** "It is summer when Earth is closer to the Sun." Wrong. Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during Northern Hemisphere winter. The tilt causes the seasons.

> **Common mistake:** "Earth's axis tips back and forth during the year." Wrong. The axis keeps pointing in the same direction in space all year. Only Earth's position in its orbit changes.

> **Common mistake:** "Days are longer in summer because Earth spins more slowly." Wrong. Earth's spin rate does not change with the seasons.

> **Common mistake:** "The longest day of the year is the hottest day." Wrong. The hottest weather comes several weeks later because of seasonal lag.

> **Common mistake:** "It is summer everywhere on Earth at the same time." Wrong. The two hemispheres always have opposite seasons.

> **Common mistake:** "Seasons are opposite in the eastern and western halves of the world." Wrong. The dividing line is the equator, not a line between east and west.

## Checkpoint quiz

Time limit: 10 minutes for 5 questions.

1. Find the noon Sun altitude at latitude 20 on the December solstice, in degrees. Answer: 46.5

2. A student says the Southern Hemisphere has summer in December because it is closer to the Sun then. What actually causes summer there? Answer: The Southern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun.

3. True or false: North of the Arctic Circle, the Sun does not set on the June solstice. Answer: True

4. A city at latitude 60 gets 18.5 hours of daylight on the June solstice. How many hours of night does it get? Answer: 5.5

5. Which place has the higher noon Sun on the June solstice?
   - A. A city at latitude 45
   - B. A city at latitude -45
   - C. Both are the same
   - D. It depends on the longitude

   Answer: A
